item.title: THE ‘INTERNAL MARKET DETOUR’ FOR DEFENDING DEMOCRACY [pre-publication]
item.description:
This article examines the EU’s recent approach to defending democracy through internal market legislation. It analyses three central instruments – the European Media Freedom Act, the Political Advertising Regulation and the proposed Transparency of Foreign Interest Directive – to show how their political aim of defending democracy comes into tension with their market-centric legal basis in Article 114 TFEU. The article argues that this ‘internal market detour’ is legally sustainable, but normatively ambivalent. While it enables the EU to act in areas where it lacks explicit competences, the approach of channelling the defence of democracy through the language and logic of the internal market also comes with adverse effects, such as reducing democratic actors to market participants. Drawing on deliberative democracy theory, the article frames the ‘internal market detour’ as a ‘tragic choice’ for the European legislature: a path that allows proactive regulatory action in defence of democracy, but at the cost of transparency and democratic expressivity.

item.title: UPCYCLING AND TRADE MARK USE UNDER EU LAW [pre-publication]
item.description:
Over the past few years, the environmental toll of the fashion industry has prompted the European Union to adopt measures aimed at fostering circularity and extending product lifecycles. As a result, design methods that repurpose garments otherwise destined for landfill – most notably, upcycling – have gained momentum as both a sustainable and fashionable practice. Yet when upcycled items retain visible brand insignia, they often risk encroaching upon the scope of trade mark protection, triggering infringement claims. This article takes a step back from the already recommended approaches and revisits a more fundamental question: does upcycling even entail ‘use’ of a trade mark in the sense required under EU law? Re-examining the Court of Justice’s case law, the main tenet of this contribution is that several forms of sustainability-oriented upcycling may not reach this threshold, as upcyclers typically do not engage in the kind of active conduct required by the law to qualify as ‘use’. The article thus positions the notion of ‘use’ as a conceptual filter that reconciles trade mark protection with circular-economy objectives. By showing that the existing framework already contains the tools to exclude genuinely sustainable repurposing from infringement – while still capturing parasitic practices – it clarifies how EU trade mark law can reconcile environmental innovation with trade mark owners’ interests and do so without the need for legislative intervention.

item.title: BETWEEN INTERNATIONAL OBLIGATIONS AND REALPOLITIK: HOW THE EU RESPONDS – AND HOW IT SHOULD RESPOND – TO UNLAWFUL OCCUPATIONS AND ANNEXATIONS [pre-publication]
item.description:
The European Union has long been confronted with unlawful occupations and annexations in its neighbourhood, situations that test the coherence, credibility and legality of its external action. This article examines the EU’s responses to such territorial situationsin light of the international obligations binding on international organizations, in particular the duties of nonrecognition and non-assistance. It shows that while these obligations appear straightforward, their implementation is constrained by political, economic and strategic considerations that generate uneven and sometimes inconsistent EU practice. The analysis identifies the legal techniques through which the EU has sought to give effect to its international obligations when confronted with unlawful occupations and annexations, the areas in which it has fallen short, and the ways in which its practice in this domain has contributed to the development of international law. The article argues that moral, political and strategic considerations provide compelling reasons for a more principled and consistent EU approach to such territorial situations.

Balancing national and EU-level enforcement in EU consumer law reform: The case of the UCPD and dark patterns
item.description:
This article aims to analyse the unfolding developments in EU consumer law, which point towards the adoption of a new law entitled the Digital Fairness Act. This act, in parallel with the revision of the Consumer Protection Cooperation Regulation, plans to address the consumer law challenges of the digital economy. The article delves into the questionable approach adopted by the European Commission, which sees the solution to the digital economy’s consumer problems in adopting a legislative act, hand in hand with some degree of centralization favouring the Commission. This article argues that the challenges identified by the Commission cannot be overcome with new legislative means and the method of establishing exclusive EU competence in certain instances, and that a competence-sharing mechanism similar to that found in EU competition law is suitable to address these new challenges. This should be paired with the empowerment of public consumer protection agencies at national level, modelled on the ECN+ Directive.

item.title: Cumulative application of free movement law and fundamental rights in the ‘derogation situation’: A multidimensional challenge
item.description:
This article examines the evolving interaction between free movement law and the Charter of Fundamental Rights in ‘derogation situations’ where Member States must comply with fundamental rights when justifying restrictions on free movement. It shows that the recent case law of the Court of Justice of the European Union reveals two significant trends: the increasing cumulative application of substantively overlapping norms, leading to normative layering, and a growing autonomy of fundamental rights review, particularly through the identification of separate infringements in infringement proceedings. The article addresses two central questions: when, and how, should free movement provisions and fundamental rights be applied cumulatively in such situations? It argues that cumulative application is justified only where the norms are substantively distinct and fulfil a genuine diagnostic function, in line with the lex specialis logic reflected in Article 52(2) of the Charter. It also highlights the emergence of a more symbolic use of EU law provisions, notably Article 2 TEU. The article concludes by proposing a more structured methodological framework to guide the Court’s reasoning, particularly as regards the scope of ‘derogation situations’ under Article 51(1), the conduct of justification and proportionality review, and the formulation of findings of infringement.
